title: SWS
excerpt: SWS is Dutch text slang for "sowieso": definitely, anyway or for sure.
example: "I'm SWS coming to the borrel," she texted back.
text: Sowieso is one of those Dutch words that works everywhere. It can mean definitely, anyway or in any case. Typing it takes too long, so students write SWS. Context tells you which meaning they want.

title: Talking stage
excerpt: The talking stage is the early phase where you text a lot and get to know each other, before you are really dating.
example: "Are you two together?" "No, we're still in the talking stage."
text: In the talking stage you text, flirt and go on the odd date. The lines are often blurry. Nobody knows exactly what it is. After a while it turns into a relationship, a situationship or just ends.

title: TBH
excerpt: TBH stands for to be honest.
example: "TBH I didn't think that film was very good at all."
text: You put TBH in front of an honest confession, opinion or compliment. It is used a lot in texts and comments. It is close to NGL.

title: Tea
excerpt: Tea means juicy news or gossip that you want to share.
example: "Okay, I have tea," she said meaningfully at the kitchen table.
text: Spilling the tea means sharing the gossip. The term comes from drag culture, where T stood for truth. In a student house the best tea gets shared in the kitchen, late at night.

title: Tellie
excerpt: Tellie is Dutch slang for your phone. Short for "telefoon".
example: "I can't find it, where's my tellie?" he shouted through the house.
text: It is the short, casual version of telefoon. Confusing for British people, because for them a telly is a TV. In a Dutch student house, the tellie is never far away.

title: Tenta
excerpt: Tenta is Dutch student slang for an exam. Short for "tentamen".
example: "Two more tenta's to go this week," she sighed, exhausted.
text: Dutch universities split the year into blocks that end with tenta's. Fail one and you get a her, a resit. Get a 5.5 and you have a studententien: just enough to pass.

title: Tetteren
excerpt: Tetteren means partying hard and drinking a lot on a night out.
example: They had been tetteren all night until the sun came up again.
text: It is often used for a night that got completely out of hand, in a good way. A lot like doorhalen. The day after usually comes with a very brak Sunday.

title: Thesis
excerpt: A thesis is the big research project or paper you write to finish your degree.
example: "I've been working on my thesis for three months and I still haven't come up with a title."
text: What a thesis is exactly differs per country and programme. Usually it is about a clear research question and a big report. In the Netherlands it is called a scriptie. Handing it in is usually followed by a big party, the afstubo.

title: Thirst trap
excerpt: A thirst trap is a sexy or teasing photo or video someone posts to get attention and compliments.
example: "He posted a shirtless mirror selfie with the caption 'just a normal Tuesday'. Obvious thirst trap."
text: In this slang, thirst means craving attention. The trap is the photo itself. Whoever falls for it and replies flirty is thirsty. Sometimes people post a thirst trap to make an ex jealous.

title: Thirsty
excerpt: Being thirsty means you are desperate for attention, validation or romantic interest.
example: "He comments three fire emojis under every photo she posts. Very thirsty."
text: Thirsty can be about someone openly looking for attention or clearly showing they like someone. It is usually said as a tease. A photo posted for attention is a thirst trap. The Dutch would say berig.

title: THTH
excerpt: THTH is short for thuisthuis: your parents' home, as opposed to your student house.
example: "Going to THTH this weekend," she texted her housemates.
text: For Dutch students "thuis" (home) means the student house. So your parents' place gets a double home: thuisthuis. THTH is the lazy version for texting.

title: Thuis
excerpt: Thuis (home) is what Dutch students call their student house, not their parents' place.
example: "I'm going home," she said, meaning her student house and not her parents.
text: Once you move out, your student house becomes thuis. Your parents' house becomes thuisthuis. Confusing at first. Totally logical after a few weeks.

title: Thuisthuis
excerpt: Thuisthuis (home home) is your parents' house, to tell it apart from your student house.
example: At weekends he always went back to his thuisthuis for a proper hot meal.
text: The word exists because thuis is already taken by the student house. Thuisthuis is where the fridge is always full and someone does your laundry. Many Dutch students go there every weekend.

title: Tijgerpunten
excerpt: Tijgerpunten (tiger points) are a scoring system Dutch students use to compare sexual experiences.
example: "So how many tijgerpunten do you have?" he asked during the borrel.
text: You fill in a list of questions and get a number of points. It is the opposite of pandapunten, which count how long you have gone without. Mostly a drunk party game. Answer at your own risk.

title: Tjak
excerpt: Tjak is Dutch student slang for filth, like mould or old leftovers.
example: "What tjak in this kitchen," she sighed when she saw the counter.
text: Tjak covers everything from mould to food that has been lying around way too long. Every student house has a corner of tjak somewhere. Usually in the ijskast.

title: TMI
excerpt: TMI stands for too much information. You say it when someone shares more than you wanted to know.
example: "TMI!" she shouted when he shared way too many details about his date.
text: You use it when someone shares more details than wanted in a conversation. Usually something too personal. Said with a laugh, most of the time.

title: Toko
excerpt: Toko is what Dutch students call any small takeaway place whose name they don't know, like a kebab shop.
example: After going out they walked to the toko around the corner.
text: Originally a toko is an Indonesian shop. Students use it for any small food place, especially the kebab or shawarma spot you end up at after a night out. Nobody knows its real name. Everyone knows where it is.

title: Touch grass
excerpt: Touch grass means: go outside. You say it to someone who is way too into the internet.
example: "You've been upset about a stranger's comment on Reddit for two hours. Touch grass."
text: Touch grass is a funny or rude reminder to go offline. Away from online drama and back to real life. People often say it to someone who is chronically online.

title: Toxic relationship
excerpt: A toxic relationship keeps coming back to unhealthy patterns, like manipulation, control or constant fighting.
example: "They fight every week, he checks her phone and she can't go out without him. That's a toxic relationship."
text: One fight doesn't make a relationship toxic. It is about a pattern of disrespect, control or manipulation. Think gaslighting and love bombing. Talk about it with someone you trust.

title: Tranqi
excerpt: Tranqi is short for tranquilo, Spanish for calm or chill. Dutch students use it to tell someone to relax.
example: "Tranqi, it'll be fine," she told her stressed housemate.
text: The short version is just a bit faster to say than tranquilo, but means exactly the same. Very useful during exam week.

title: Tranquilo
excerpt: Tranquilo is Spanish for calm or chill. Dutch students use it to tell someone to calm down.
example: "Tranquilo, it's all going to be fine," she said to calm her friend before the exam.
text: You use it when someone drank too much or is stressing out. Dutch students borrowed it from Spanish and never gave it back. Short version: tranqi.

title: Trekken
excerpt: Trekken (to pull) is Dutch student slang for downing a drink in one go, like in bak trekken.
example: "Just trek it," she said when he hesitated over his beer.
text: Students mostly use trekken in the sense of bak trekken: finishing a drink, beer or Smirnoff Ice in one go. In English you would say chug or down it.

title: Trending
excerpt: Trending means a topic, hashtag or video is really popular right now and lots of people are talking about it.
example: "That dance is trending, half the association did it at the party."
text: Platforms like TikTok and X keep track of what is trending. A trend can be a song, a challenge or a meme. Often a trend only lasts a few days. After that it is already cringe.

title: Troll
excerpt: A troll is someone who deliberately provokes or annoys people online to get a reaction.
example: "Don't reply. That guy is just trolling."
text: Trolling means provoking with fake opinions, insults or nonsense. The goal is chaos or anger. Among friends, trolling can also just be a harmless joke. The best advice is still: don't feed the troll.

title: Turflijst
excerpt: A turflijst (tally list), also called streeplijst, keeps track of how many drinks every housemate had.
example: The old turflijst of their student house still hung next to the fridge.
text: Everyone puts a stripe behind their name for every beer they take from the house stock. At the end of the month you settle up. The paper system is a bit old-school, but some houses keep the tradition alive. Apps have taken over in most places.

title: Tutorial
excerpt: A tutorial is a class in a small group or one on one, where you discuss the material. Online it is also an explainer video.
example: "In the tutorial it turned out I was the only one who hadn't read the article."
text: A tutorial is more personal and interactive than a lecture. What it means exactly differs per university. Online, tutorial also means a step-by-step explainer video, like a make-up tutorial.

title: UB
excerpt: The UB ("universiteitsbibliotheek") is the university library, where Dutch students study and borrow books.
example: She spent the whole week studying for her exam in the UB.
text: During exam weeks the UB is packed and finding a seat is a sport. Some students show up at opening time to get one. In Leiden it has a nickname of its own: the LUL.

title: Uf
excerpt: A uf (or ufje) is a member of the UVSV, the women's student association in Utrecht.
example: As a uf she joined the introduction week of her association every year.
text: The nickname refers specifically to members of the UVSV, the Utrecht Women's Student Association. It is one of the biggest student associations in the Netherlands. The closest thing in the US would be a sorority.

title: Unhinged
excerpt: Unhinged means completely over the top, chaotic or totally unpredictable.
example: "She sent a ten-minute voice memo to the group chat at four in the morning. Unhinged."
text: Literally unhinged means taken off its hinges. It can be negative, but it is often meant as a joke. Unhinged humour is absurd and over the top. An unhinged night was wild and chaotic.

title: Unpopular opinion
excerpt: An unpopular opinion is an opinion you think most people won't agree with.
example: "Unpopular opinion: a night in is better than going out."
text: You see unpopular opinions all over social media. Often the opinion turns out way more popular than expected. It is close to a hot take.

title: Valid
excerpt: Valid means something is understandable, fair or okay.
example: "I'm not coming tonight, I'm just tired." "Valid."
text: Online you say valid to show someone's opinion, choice or feeling makes sense. You accept it without arguing. It is short, supportive and relaxed.

title: Vanaaf
excerpt: Vanaaf is Dutch text slang for "vanavond": tonight.
example: "What are we doing vanaaf?" she texted the group around dinner time.
text: It is the short, casual way to write vanavond. You will see it in almost every Dutch group chat. Usually followed by a plan, a location and a lot of bee emojis.

title: Vestjeslikker
excerpt: A vestjeslikker (vest licker) is someone who is mostly interested in board members or prominent members because of their status.
example: "Don't be such a vestjeslikker," they joked when he was being way too nice to the board.
text: Board members of Dutch associations often wear special vests or jackets. A vestjeslikker is drawn to those, romantically or socially, because of the status that comes with them. Basically clout chasing, association style.

title: Veto
excerpt: Using your veto means blocking a proposal, for example at a meeting of a Dutch student association.
example: During the ALV she unexpectedly used her veto against the proposal.
text: Veto is Latin for "I forbid". Within a dispuut or student house, one veto can be enough to stop a new member from being voted in. A lot of power in one word.

title: Vibe
excerpt: A vibe is the atmosphere, mood or energy a person, place or situation gives off.
example: "I don't know why, but that bar just has a good vibe."
text: Vibe is a vague word on purpose. You use it for atmosphere, a click, a style or a gut feeling. Someone can give off good vibes or a weird vibe. Testing if something feels right is a vibe check.

title: Vibe check
excerpt: A vibe check is a casual test of whether someone or something feels right and fits the mood.
example: "New housemate? First a vibe check over dinner."
text: Online, vibe check is often used as a joke. Like a meme where someone shouts "vibe check" and does something weird. In normal conversations it just means feeling out someone or a situation. A Dutch hospi is basically one big vibe check.

title: Vino
excerpt: Vino is Spanish for wine. Dutch students use it for pretty much every occasion.
example: "Passed your tenta? Time for vino!" she shouted.
text: Passed or failed, celebrating or sad, there is always a reason for vino. Part of the little family of Spanish words Dutch students love, together with bueno and tranquilo.

title: Viral
excerpt: Going viral means a post, video or meme spreads across the internet super fast.
example: "His video of the failed chug went viral. Two million views in one day."
text: Viral comes from virus, because the content spreads just as fast. People share it with friends, who send it on again. One viral moment can make someone famous overnight. Or get them cancelled.

title: Vo
excerpt: Vo is short for bravo. At Dutch student associations people shout it instead of clapping.
example: "Vo!" his dispuut shouted when he finished his speech.
text: At many student associations people shout vo instead of applauding, or to show respect when someone says something good. Expect a loud chorus of vo's after every speech.

title: Vozen
excerpt: Vozen is Dutch student slang for making out: kissing and touching.
example: They were vozen on the dance floor all night.
text: It covers kissing, often with some touching. A bit less crude than huig hockeyen. You will hear it mostly in stories the morning after.

title: Vrijmibo
excerpt: Vrijmibo (short for "vrijdagmiddagborrel") is the Friday afternoon drinks to close the week.
example: Every Friday at five the vrijmibo started at the sociëteit.
text: Students use it to close the study week, workers to leave the work week behind. Lots of Dutch offices have one too. A borrel, by the way, is the Dutch word for casual drinks with snacks. Very gezellig.

title: VVV'tje
excerpt: A VVV'tje (short for "vriendje van vroeger") is a friend from before your student years.
example: At the party she suddenly ran into an old VVV'tje from her home town.
text: It is a friendship that exists outside your association or student house, from before you started studying. The friends from school or your village who knew you before all the slang.

title: W
excerpt: W stands for win. You use it for something good, a victory or someone who does well.
example: "The bar has free bitterballen tonight. Big W."
text: W comes from gaming, where a W is a game you won. Now you say it about anything that turns out well. The opposite is an L.

title: Walk of shame
excerpt: The walk of shame is the trip home in the morning after a night at someone else's place, still in last night's clothes.
example: "At nine I saw her walking past the bakery in a glitter dress and heels. The classic walk of shame."
text: Everyone can tell from your outfit that you didn't sleep at home. A hangover often comes with it. These days lots of people call it the stride of pride instead. Nothing to be ashamed of, they say.

title: Wegtikken
excerpt: Wegtikken means knocking back beers at a really high pace.
example: During the contest he was wegtikken his beers in record time.
text: It is a lot like bakken vouwen or pinten harken. All ways to drink a lot of beer fast. Dutch students clearly needed many words for this.

title: Wild
excerpt: You say wild when something is surprising, extreme or unbelievable.
example: "He visited three cities in one night and lost his passport? Wild."
text: Wild is a flexible reaction word. You use it to show shock, surprise or amusement. A wild night is a night that got out of hand. It is close to unhinged and chaotic.

title: Wingman
excerpt: A wingman helps you start a good conversation with someone on a night out.
example: As a wingman he made sure his friend finally dared to talk to her.
text: A wingman is a friend who helps you start a fun conversation, especially when you find that hard yourself. They hype you up, keep the friends busy and know when to disappear. Not everyone has rizz. Everyone can have a wingman.

title: Work-life balance
excerpt: Work-life balance is the balance between work or studies and rest, relationships, health and your private life.
example: "I study, work twenty hours and I'm on a committee. My work-life balance is nowhere to be found."
text: There is no perfect formula. A good balance means work doesn't push everything else aside all the time. Time for friends, sports and sleep is part of it. It is the opposite of hustle culture.

title: WTF
excerpt: WTF stands for what the fuck. You use it when you are shocked, confused or can't believe something.
example: "WTF, who put the couch in the garden?"
text: WTF is really common online, but it is rude. So you don't use it in formal emails or at work. A moment you really didn't see coming is a WTF moment.

title: X
excerpt: X can mean a digital kiss at the end of a message. It is also slang for the drug ecstasy.
example: At the end of the text she quickly added an x, just to be sweet.
text: At the end of a message, x means a kiss. Dutch people use it a lot, even with friends. As slang, X also means ecstasy pills, with MDMA as the active ingredient. The Dutch call the powder version M.

title: Yap
excerpt: Yapping means talking non-stop, often about anything and everything.
example: "Sorry for the nine-minute voice memo. I was yapping again."
text: Yap comes from a small barking dog. Online people use it jokingly about themselves for talking way too long. Someone who always talks is a yapper. It is usually meant lightly.

title: YOLO
excerpt: YOLO stands for You Only Live Once. You only live once, so why not?
example: "Another round of shots on a Tuesday? YOLO."
text: YOLO got big in 2011 through the song The Motto by Drake. You shout it as an excuse for a spontaneous or unwise choice. It is close to FOMO, but YOLO is about daring, not about being afraid to miss out.

title: Zeester
excerpt: Zeester (starfish) is Dutch student slang for the passive partner during sex.
example: "In bed she was a real zeester," people said about her.
text: Picture a starfish lying on its back. That is the idea. It is used for the person who stays passive during sex. Not a compliment, and mostly heard in gossip.

title: Zombieing
excerpt: Zombieing is when someone who ghosted you suddenly gets back in touch.
example: "Three months of nothing and now he sends 'hey stranger'. Classic zombieing."
text: Just like a zombie, the person comes back from the dead. Often when the contact seemed long gone. An explanation rarely follows. It is part of the family of ghosting, orbiting and breadcrumbing.
